Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the GreenWave Energy Corp. Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. Participants are reminded that questions should be submitted via the dial-in star key followed by one. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss GreenWave Energy Corp.'s results for the Q3 2024. Joining me on today's call are Jordan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; Taylor Voss, Chief Financial Officer; and Morgan Lee, Chief Development Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call will contain forward-looking statements. We encourage you to review the disclaimer in our press release and on our website regarding these statements.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Jordan Hale.

Jordan Hale:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. GreenWave Energy Corp. delivered a solid performance in the Q3, driven by strong execution and growing demand for our renewable energy solutions. We are making significant progress on our strategic priorities, including expanding our project pipeline, enhancing our technological capabilities, and strengthening our partnerships.

I'd like to highlight four key aspects of our performance this quarter.

First, our overall performance highlights and key achievements. Taylor, please walk us through the details.

Taylor Voss:
Thank you, Jordan, and good afternoon, everyone. I'm pleased to dive into our Q3 results, which underscore GreenWave Energy Corp.'s position as a leader in the integrated renewables and clean tech ecosystem. For the quarter ended September 30th, we delivered record performance across the board, driven by robust demand for our utility-scale solar, onshore wind, and long-duration energy storage solutions amid accelerating global electrification and decarbonization mandates.

Starting with the top line: consolidated revenue reached $478 million, up 35% year-over-year and 10% quarter-over-quarter, surpassing our guidance midpoint by 7%. This marks our ninth straight quarter of double-digit growth, fueled by a 42% surge in project EPC revenue to $310 million and a 28% increase in our O&M services backlog to $2.1 billion. Recurring revenue from power purchase agreements and asset optimization now comprises 25% of total revenue—up from 18% a year ago—reflecting the maturation of our 3.2 GW owned-and-operated portfolio, which generated $135 million in stable cash flows at an average PPA tenor of 18 years.

On profitability, adjusted EBITDA hit $142 million, delivering a class-leading 29.7% margin—expanding 280 basis points YoY. This was propelled by economies of scale in our module procurement, where we locked in fixed-price contracts for 1.8 GW of high-efficiency TOPCon bifacial panels at an average $0.21 per watt, 18% below spot market levels amid stabilizing polysilicon prices post the 2023 oversupply correction. Free cash flow before growth capex came in at $110 million, up 48% YoY, enabling $52 million in shareholder returns via our expanded buyback program and a 15% dividend hike to $0.21 per share.

Key achievements this quarter highlight our execution prowess and strategic foresight. We achieved commercial operation on our flagship 550 MW Rattlesnake Solar + Storage project in Texas' ERCOT market, integrating 200 MWh of our proprietary LFP-based EcoFlow battery systems with 28% DC:AC ratio optimization via AI-driven curtailment forecasting. This hybrid facility, backed by a 15-year PPA with Luminant, is already delivering 25% higher capacity factors than standalone solar peers, thanks to our advanced string inverters from partnerships like Sungrow. In total, we commissioned 1.4 GW across our pipeline—65% solar, 25% wind, 10% storage—bringing YTD deployments to 2.8 GW.

We also inked two landmark deals: a $1.4 billion EPC contract for a 450 MW portfolio in California's CAISO grid, incorporating our next-gen perovskite-silicon tandem modules with 32% lab efficiencies scaling to commercial pilots; and a 350 MW wind repower in the Midwest PJM zone, leveraging our Vestas Platinum partnership for 5.5 MW turbines with 60% capacity factors. Our development backlog now stands at $6.2 billion, with 72% contracted and an expected IRR of 12-14% post-tax credits.

Technical and innovation initiatives saw R&D spend rise 20% to $25 million, yielding breakthroughs like our GridSync AI platform, now deployed across 1.8 GW of assets, which has reduced imbalance penalties by 40% and boosted ancillary services revenue by $22 million YTD—mirroring trends seen at peers like NextEra. We're also advancing green hydrogen integration, with our 60 MW electrolyzer pilot at the Rattlesnake site producing 2,500 tons annually at $2.40/kg, positioning us ahead of the curve as DOE's Hydrogen Hubs ramp up.

Regionally, in the U.S., which accounts for 72% of revenue, IRA-driven ITC/PTC adders and state-level mandates propelled 48% YoY growth, with Texas and California representing 40% of new bookings despite interconnection queues easing to 18 months via FERC Order 2023. Europe contributed 20% of revenue, up 52% on REPowerEU funding; our 300 MW Dutch offshore wind stake with Ørsted exemplifies this, though grid bottlenecks persist. APAC saw 32% growth via a 180 MW rooftop solar MSA in India, hedging China supply chain risks through Vietnam diversification—our module localization now at 38% for tariff resilience.

Strategically, amid LCOE declines—solar now at $25-30/MWh unsubsidized per Lazard's 2024 analysis—we're capitalizing on storage mandates, targeting 1.2 GW annual additions through 2027. Supply chain resilience remains core: our 2.5 GW U.S. Balance of System factory in Arizona de-risks Section 201/301 tariffs, yielding 16% cost savings. ESG-wise, our portfolio avoided 4.8 million metric tons of CO2e YTD, earning S&P's top sustainability score and unlocking $350 million in green bond financing at 4.1% yields.

Looking ahead, Q4 revenue guidance is $500-530 million with EBITDA margins of 28-30%, supported by $2.8 billion liquidity and a net debt:EBITDA of 1.7x. We're raising our FY24 outlook by 6% to $2.1 billion in revenue. These results affirm our "Build, Own, Optimize" model in a market projected to add 500 GW globally per IRENA.

Thank you, Jordan. Back to you on the next aspect.

Jordan Hale:
Thanks, Taylor. Second, our development pipeline additions and project milestones, which Morgan will detail.

Morgan Lee:
Thank you, Jordan. Moving now to our development pipeline additions and project milestones, which continue to underscore our leadership in the clean tech space. As many of you know, our pipeline is a critical leading indicator for future revenue growth, representing over 20 GW of advanced-stage projects across solar PV, onshore and offshore wind, battery energy storage systems—or BESS—and emerging green hydrogen initiatives. In Q3 alone, we added a robust 4.8 GW to our global development pipeline, bringing our total to 28.2 GW as of quarter-end. This represents a 22% quarter-over-quarter increase and positions us in the top quartile among peers like NextEra Energy Resources and Ørsted, based on S&P Global Platts data.

Let me break this down by technology and region for clarity. Starting with solar PV, which remains our largest bucket at 55% of the total pipeline or 15.5 GW. We added 2.9 GW this quarter, primarily from utility-scale greenfield additions in the U.S. Southwest and Australia. Key here is our shift toward next-gen bifacial TOPCon modules with efficiencies exceeding 23%, sourced via long-term offtake agreements with tier-1 suppliers like LONGi and JinkoSolar. These modules, paired with single-axis trackers from Nextracker, are delivering LCOEs—levelized costs of energy—as low as $25/MWh in high-irradiance regions, down 15% year-over-year due to module price deflation and improved bifacial gains averaging 25-30% rear-side yield.

On the wind side, we bolstered our portfolio by 1.2 GW, split evenly between onshore and offshore. Our onshore additions—600 MW—are concentrated in the U.S. Midwest, leveraging the Inflation Reduction Act's PTC—Production Tax Credit—extensions and transferability provisions, which have accelerated our monetization strategy. Notably, we're deploying GE Vernova's 6.1 MW onshore turbines with 155-meter rotors for enhanced AEP—annual energy production—in low-wind regimes. Offshore, the 600 MW addition stems from our progression on the Gulf of Maine Floating Wind Project, a 1.2 GW phased development where we've secured an anchor tenant with Eversource and advanced to FEED—front-end engineering and design—with Equinor as a technical partner. Floating wind is a high-conviction bet for us; global capacity is projected to hit 5 GW by 2026 per IRENA, and our pipeline here gives us early-mover advantage in U.S. waters.

BESS saw the strongest growth at 35% YoY, with 450 MW / 900 MWh added, pushing our total storage pipeline to 3.8 GW / 10.2 GWh. This aligns with the grid stability crunch amid renewables penetration exceeding 40% in key ISO markets like CAISO and ERCOT. We're focusing on four-hour lithium-iron-phosphate systems from CATL and Tesla Megapack integrations, but with a twist: 20% of new additions incorporate long-duration flow batteries using Form Energy's iron-air tech, targeting 100+ hour dispatch for renewables curtailment mitigation.

Finally, our green hydrogen foray added 250 MW of electrolyzer capacity equivalent, tied to our Texas Blue Hydrogen Hub project. This leverages DOE's Regional Clean Hydrogen Hubs funding—we're in the running for $1.2B in Phase 2 grants—and positions us for offtake from industrial loads like CF Industries' ammonia plants.

Regionally, the U.S. dominates at 42% of additions (2.0 GW), fueled by IRA-driven capex tax credits yielding effective ITC yields up to 50-70% for solar-plus-storage hybrids. Europe contributed 28% (1.3 GW), with strong momentum in Spain and Italy under REPowerEU's 320 GW solar target by 2030. Grid bottlenecks persist—ENTSO-E reports 15 GW of queued projects facing delays—but our 1.1 GW of Spanish additions secured grid slots via early auctions. APAC at 20% (1.0 GW) reflects Australia's Capacity Investment Scheme and India's 500 GW non-fossil target, where we're partnering with Adani Green on hybrid solar-wind farms. Emerging markets like Latin America (10%, 500 MW) tap Brazil's hybrid auctions, with our first 200 MW solar-BESS PPA signed with Petrobras.

Turning to project milestones, Q3 was execution-heavy, de-risking 3.2 GW across the pipeline. We hit financial close on 1.1 GW of U.S. projects, raising $1.8B in non-recourse debt at blended rates of 4.2%—50 bps tighter than Q2, thanks to improved DSCRs—debt service coverage ratios—averaging 1.6x from conservative P50 energy yields. Tax equity commitments totaled $900M, fully subscribed by funds like GE Vernova Financial Services.

Construction kicked off—or NTP issued—on 1.5 GW, including our flagship Avalon Solar + Storage (500 MWdc / 1 GWh) in Arizona, where EPC is 15% complete with first pour milestone hit. This project's PPA with APS at $22/MWh fixed exemplifies our contracted backlog strength—85% of pipeline now has PPAs or LOIs, up from 72% last year, mitigating merchant exposure amid PPA prices softening 10-15% in oversupplied markets.

Interconnection and permitting advanced on 650 MW, with FERC queue reforms in PJM and MISO clearing two projects (400 MW total) from study phases. In Europe, we secured environmental approvals for our 300 MW Dutch offshore lease area, aligning with North Sea Wind Plan targets.

Looking ahead, Q4 milestones include COD on 800 MW of backlog—400 MW U.S. solar and 400 MW Australian BESS—unlocking $450M in revenue recognition under IFRS 15. We're targeting NTP on another 2 GW by year-end, with offshore FID—final investment decision—for Gulf of Maine Phase 1 in H1 2025.

Strategically, these additions reflect our three-pillar approach: (1) technology diversification to hedge commodity risks—solar/wind correlation dropped to 0.4 in our portfolio via BESS and hydrogen; (2) merchant optimization—15% of new U.S. pipeline targets California LCFS credits and Texas ERCOT scarcity pricing, where peaks hit $5,000/MWh this summer; and (3) supply chain resilience—80% domestic content for IRA compliance, with U.S. module manufacturing ramping via First Solar partnerships.

Risks remain: supply chain volatility from China's 80% module dominance, potential U.S. policy shifts post-election, and European grid capex delays. But with ROIC on new projects at 12-15%, IRR hurdles cleared, and a $15B liquidity runway, we're executing flawlessly.

Thank you. Back to Jordan.

Jordan Hale:
Excellent update, Morgan. Third, PPA pricing trends and contract extensions. Taylor, over to you.

Taylor Voss:
Thank you, Jordan. Good afternoon, everyone. Before we move further, I'd like to dive deeper into two critical areas driving our long-term revenue visibility: PPA pricing trends and contract extensions. As many of you know, Power Purchase Agreements—or PPAs—are the bedrock of our business model here at GreenWave, underpinning over 85% of our 12 GW operating portfolio across solar, wind, and hybrid battery storage projects. In this high-interest-rate environment, we've seen meaningful shifts that position us favorably for the back half of 2024 and beyond.

Let me start with PPA pricing trends. Coming into 2023, we witnessed a temporary softening in U.S. PPA prices due to aggressive module price declines—Chinese Tier 1 bifacial PERC and TOPCon panels dropped to under $0.25/W—and a surge in developer supply, pushing utility-scale solar PPAs in ERCOT to as low as $22/MWh on a levelized basis. Wind was similar, with Plains states averaging $25-28/MWh amid turbine oversupply from Vestas and Siemens Gamesa.

However, Q3 marked an inflection point. PPA prices have firmed up significantly—up 18% year-over-year across our U.S. pipeline—driven by three key factors: (1) persistent inflation in EPC costs, now running at 8-10% for balance-of-system components like racking and inverters; (2) higher debt service costs amid the Fed's terminal rate around 5.25-5.50%, which has compressed IRRs from 8-9% to 6.5-7.5% for new-builds; and (3) interconnection queue bottlenecks in high-demand ISOs like CAISO and PJM, where our 2.5 GW queued capacity benefits from early positioning.

Regionally, this plays out differently. In ERCOT, where we have 1.8 GW operating, solar PPAs averaged $32/MWh for new contracts signed in Q3, a 22% premium over 2023 lows, thanks to battery-hybrid mandates and the biennial IRP refresh. Our 300 MW Rattlesnake Solar + 150 MWh BESS project just closed at $34/MWh fixed for 15 years, with a 2.5% annual escalator tied to CPI. Contrast that with PJM, where prices held steady at $38-42/MWh due to MOPR reforms and nuclear subsidies crowding out cheap renewables—our 400 MW hybrid wind-solar PPA there fetched $41/MWh, blending 35% capacity factor wind with 28% solar DC:AC ratios optimized via NREL's SAM modeling.

Internationally, Europe tells a bifurcated story. In sunny Spain and Italy, Enel and Iberdrola's aggressive builds have kept prices at €25-30/MWh ($27-33), but Germany's EEG auctions saw record highs of €55/MWh ($60) for repowered onshore wind, reflecting the Energiewende's repowering boom. We've leveraged this with a 200 MW portfolio extension in the Nordics at SEK 0.45/kWh ($0.043/kWh), capitalizing on Ørsted-like hybrid offshore strategies.

On the corporate side, hyperscalers like Google and Amazon—now 40% of our new PPA volume—have driven premiums, paying 10-15% above utility tariffs for additionality and Scope 2 matching. Our 150 MW deal with a Big Tech name in Arizona locked in $45/MWh with dynamic pricing linked to PJM Locational Marginal Prices for merchant upside.

Shifting to contract extensions, this has been a standout for us in Q3, adding 1.2 GW to our backlog at an average 25% pricing uplift over expiring legacy contracts. With 3 GW of first-generation PPAs maturing through 2025—mostly 2008-2012 vintage wind at sub-$25/MWh—we've executed extensions on 65% of eligible capacity, extending tenors by 7-10 years to 2035+.

Take our 500 MW Midwest wind fleet: Legacy PPAs at $23/MWh expired this year, but we've repowered with GE 3.8-130 turbines—boosting AEP to 45% via taller hubs and leading-edge serrations—and extended with MISO at $36/MWh, a 57% increase. This includes carve-outs for 20% merchant exposure during shoulder seasons, capturing $50+/MWh spikes seen in 2022's Uri event redux.

Technical initiatives have been key enablers. We've integrated firm capacity products via co-located BESS—our 100 MW/400 MWh Mesquite storage arbitrage yields 95% dispatchable profiles, qualifying for PJM's RPM auctions at $150/kW-year. In California, SGIP-funded retrofits on 250 MW solar have unlocked LCFS credits worth $10/MWh equivalent. And our proprietary PPA optimizer tool, blending Aurora Solar forecasting with McKinsey's 2024 LCOE curves, has de-risked bids to sub-2% P90 error rates.

Strategically, we're tilting toward 10-12 year tenors with hybrid offtake—60% fixed, 40% indexed to Henry Hub gas or EU carbon prices—to hedge vol. This mirrors NextEra's playbook, where extensions now comprise 30% of their FCF. For GreenWave, these moves lift our fleet-wide implied PPA price to $37/MWh through 2030, up from $31 last year, with 92% contracted backlog.

In summary, PPA trends are normalizing to sustainable levels—$30-45/MWh band for U.S. solar/wind hybrids—while extensions lock in high-teens IRRs on brownfield assets. This gives us bulletproof visibility amid election-year policy noise, like IRA PTC extensions or EU REPowerEU deadlines. We're guiding 15-20% YoY revenue growth from these levers alone.

Jordan Hale:
Thank you, Taylor. Finally, fourth, our debt levels and financing costs—Taylor, please continue.

Taylor Voss:
Thank you, Jordan, and good afternoon, everyone. I'll now turn to our balance sheet strength, specifically our debt levels and financing costs, which continue to underpin our robust execution in the renewable energy sector. As we scale our 15 GW portfolio of utility-scale solar, onshore wind, and battery storage assets—much like our peers at NextEra Energy and Orsted—maintaining disciplined leverage while securing cost-effective capital is paramount in this capital-intensive industry.

Let me start with the headline numbers. At quarter-end, our total gross debt stood at $5.2 billion, reflecting a 5% sequential reduction from $5.5 billion in Q2, driven primarily by $350 million in principal repayments on our construction revolver and strong cash flows from stabilized assets. Net debt came in at $4.1 billion, after adjusting for $1.1 billion in unrestricted cash and equivalents. This translates to a consolidated leverage ratio of 3.2x Net Debt to trailing twelve-month Adjusted EBITDA—comfortably within our target range of 3.0x to 3.5x and below the industry average of 4.1x as reported by S&P Global for clean energy developers.

Breaking it down by composition, 72% of our debt is long-term fixed-rate, with an average maturity of 6.8 years. This includes $2.8 billion in non-recourse project financing for assets like our 800 MW Desert Sun solar-plus-storage hybrid in California and our 500 MW Atlantic Breeze offshore wind project off the U.S. East Coast. We've structured these under tax equity partnerships leveraging the Inflation Reduction Act's (IRA) enhanced Investment Tax Credits (ITC) at 40-50% effective yields, which have de-risked lender exposure and kept advance rates at 65-75%. The remaining 28% is corporate-level debt: $800 million in green bonds issued last year at a 3.8% coupon—aligned with ICMA Green Bond Principles—and a $600 million term loan A facility.

On financing costs, our full-year interest expense totaled $185 million, down 8% year-over-year, with a blended cost of debt of 4.2%—a 25 basis point improvement from 4.45% in FY '23. This was achieved through proactive refinancing initiatives. In Q3, we upsized and extended our $1.2 billion revolving credit facility—now at $1.5 billion with a $300 million accordion—from a syndicate led by BofA and JPMorgan, pricing it at SOFR + 175 bps, or effectively 5.9% post-margin. Critically, 85% of our exposure is hedged via interest rate swaps: we've fixed $2.2 billion at an all-in rate of 3.9%, shielding us from the Fed's recent 25 bps cut while positioning for further easing. For context, unhedged peers like some mid-tier solar developers are seeing effective rates north of 6% amid the lagged impact of 2022's rate hikes.

Regionally, our U.S. operations—representing 60% of debt outstanding—benefit from the IRA's clean energy incentives, enabling sub-4% project yields and strong bank appetite from players like MUFG and Société Générale. In Europe, where we have 25% exposure via our 1.2 GW portfolio in Germany and the UK, costs are slightly higher at 4.8% blended due to ECB policy divergence and REPowerEU-driven supply chain inflation, but we've locked in €500 million in sustainability-linked loans (SLLs) tied to Scope 1/2 emissions reductions, earning a 15 bps greenium. Emerging markets like our 400 MW solar pipeline in India and Brazil carry higher costs—5.5% average—but are non-recourse and backed by long-term PPAs with investment-grade offtakers, mitigating currency risks through USD-denominated tails.

Strategically, we're laser-focused on deleveraging while funding growth. Free cash flow generation hit $420 million in Q3, exceeding expectations thanks to 95%+ fleet availability and merchant upside from our 200 MWh BESS deployments capturing CAISO's ancillary services premiums. This has given us ample headroom under covenants: 25% excess availability on our corporate revolver and 2.1x debt service coverage on projects. Looking ahead, we plan to refinance $900 million in maturing term debt in H1 '25 at targeted rates below 4%, potentially via additional green bonds amid robust demand—global green bond issuance topped $500 billion in 2024 per Climate Bonds Initiative. We're also advancing battery recycling JV with Redwood Materials to monetize offtake streams, further bolstering liquidity.

In summary, our debt profile is investment-grade quality—BBB- rated by Fitch—with declining costs and prudent hedging supporting 12-15% ROIC on new builds. This positions us exceptionally well for our 3 GW backlog conversion and $2 billion capex guidance for FY '25.

Thank you, Jordan.

Jordan Hale:
Now, I'll turn the call over to Taylor to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Taylor Voss:
Thank you, Jordan. As Jordan mentioned, we had a strong financial performance in the Q3. Our revenue was $478 million, representing a 35% increase year-over-year. This growth was primarily driven by increased project commissioning and higher energy production across our portfolio. Our gross margin was 42%, reflecting improved operational efficiency and favorable pricing. Operating expenses were $145 million, primarily due to increased investments in research and development and sales and marketing. Our net income was $85 million, or $0.72 per share. We ended the quarter with $1.1 billion in cash and cash equivalents. We are reaffirming our full-year guidance for revenue and earnings.

Now, I'll turn the call back to Jordan for closing remarks.

Jordan Hale:
Thank you, Taylor. In closing, I am confident that GreenWave Energy Corp. is well-positioned to capitalize on the growing demand for renewable energy. We remain focused on executing our strategic priorities and delivering long-term value for our shareholders.

Operator, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Ladies and gentlemen, at this time we will begin the question-and-answer session. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Sarah Kline with BloombergNEF. Please go ahead.

Sarah Kline:
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of Rattlesnake Solar + Storage on your project economics?

Jordan Hale:
Good morning, Sarah. Great question on the Rattlesnake project. As we highlighted, this 550 MW solar plus 200 MWh BESS hybrid in ERCOT has transformed our project economics. The 15-year PPA at $34/MWh fixed with a 2.5% CPI escalator delivers an IRR north of 14% post-ITC, thanks to the battery co-location boosting capacity factors to over 50% blended. AI-optimized curtailment via our GridSync platform minimizes penalties, while LCFS and ancillary revenues add $8-10/MWh upside. Compared to standalone solar at $25/MWh PPAs last year, this hybrid model lifts LCOE by 20% efficiency gains and de-risks via 95% dispatchability. It's a blueprint for our 3 GW pipeline, enhancing returns amid firming prices.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mike Patel with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Mike Patel:
What are your expectations for grid connection timelines for your upcoming projects?

Morgan Lee:
Thanks, Mike. Grid timelines remain a key focus, but we're seeing improvements. In the U.S., FERC Order 2023 reforms have accelerated PJM and MISO queues—our 400 MW cleared studies this quarter, targeting 18-month connections versus 36+ months pre-reform. ERCOT's 1.8 GW operating benefits from faster processes, with Avalon Solar NTP'd for COD in 12 months. In CAISO, bottlenecks persist for 15 GW queued, but our early positioning and hybrid mandates secure slots. Europe: REPowerEU aids, but ENTSO-E delays average 24 months—our Spanish 1.1 GW and Dutch 300 MW offshore have approvals, eyeing 20 months. Overall, we expect 85% of 2 GW NTP projects to connect in 18-24 months, supported by domestic content for priority.

Operator:
[Operator Instructions] There appear to be no further questions at this time. I will now turn the call back over to Jordan Hale for any closing remarks.

Jordan Hale:
Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. We appreciate your interest in GreenWave Energy Corp. We look forward to speaking with you again next quarter.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
